01 — ABOUT

Who's in the file

I'm a second-year Computer Science student at Gordon College. My OJT started on paper — folders, forms, and a records cabinet at the Olongapo Multi-Purpose Cooperative (OMPC) — before I moved into the multimedia department to help build the cooperative's loan system online.

It wasn't the kind of "technical" experience I expected going in, at least not at first. But starting on the records side ended up shaping how I approach the digital side now — I already knew what the process needed to look like before I tried to build it.

02 — FIELD RECORD

What I actually did at OMPC

Four tasks — from paper records to building the system that replaces them.
TASK 01

Loan Note Processing

Filled out loan note forms accurately and cross-checked every entry against members' existing records — no room for a mismatch.

Learned: how much a single form can carry, and why double-checking isn't optional.

TASK 02

Folder Labeling

Labeled folders for fast retrieval. Learned fast that one mislabeled folder can cost someone an entire afternoon of searching.

Learned: naming conventions matter — for folders and for code.

TASK 03

Document Storage

Filed loan notes and organized folders into the cooperative's storage system, building a filing rhythm anyone in the office could follow.

Learned: a system only works if the next person can use it without asking you first.

TASK 04 — CURRENT

Multimedia Department: Digital Systems

Moved into the multimedia department, where I'm now building an online loan application form and an admin dashboard — taking the exact filing process I used to do by hand and turning it into software.

Learned: everything the paper system taught me about order and accuracy is directly shaping how I'm designing the digital one.

About OMPC — the Olongapo Multi-Purpose Cooperative is a financial and service cooperative based in Olongapo City, governed by the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA), offering savings, loans, and other member-driven programs.

04 — PROFESSIONAL WORK

From paper trail to the real thing

Now with the multimedia department, I'm building the digital system that replaces the exact process I used to do by hand — a public loan application form and a secured admin dashboard for OMPC's website.
PROJECT 01

Online Loan Application Form

A public-facing form for OMPC members to submit loan applications directly on the website — built to replace the paper loan note forms I used to process by hand.

Stack: Framer (frontend), Supabase (backend)

PROJECT 02

Admin Dashboard

A secured, authenticated dashboard for OMPC staff to review, filter, and manage submitted loan applications — including search, pagination, and status tracking.

Stack: React / TypeScript, Supabase Auth & RLS

SCREENSHOT — LOAN APPLICATION FORM

Public-facing member loan application form — personal info, loan details, and purpose of loan.

05 — FIELD NOTES

Reflection

I honestly didn't expect my OJT to revolve mostly around physical records — but I picked up lessons that go way beyond just coding. I got better at document management and paying attention to detail, and I learned proper office etiquette: how to communicate professionally, respect deadlines, and work well with a team that relies on accuracy. Good systems — digital or on paper — all come down to the same things: order, consistency, and genuinely caring about the details. That's the habit I'm taking with me into every project after this one, especially in data organization and systems documentation. Now I'm in the multimedia department, building an online loan application form and an admin dashboard — and it's honestly full circle. Every rule I learned from filing loan notes by hand — how forms should be checked, how records should be labeled, how a system should make sense to the next person using it — is exactly what I'm trying to build into the software version.
